newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Pakistan finish talks, agree to hold more.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan finish talks, agree to hold more.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani diplomats on Monday ended four days of talks aimed at reducing tension between the bitter South Asian rivals and agreed to meet again in the Pakistan capital Islamabad.
"The two foreign secretaries discussed all outstanding issues of concern to both sides in a frank, cordial and constructive manner," a joint statement issued after the talks said.
"The foreign secretaries decided to continue their discussions in Islamabad on dates to be mutually decided."

The negotiations between Indian Foreign Secretary Salman Haidar and his Pakistani counterpart Shamshad Ahmad were the first since similar discussions collapsed in acrimony three years ago amid deep differences over the disputed Himalayan region of Kashmir.

The latest four-day meetings coincided with renewed violence in Kashmir and political turmoil in New Delhi, where the Congress party on Sunday withdrew support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 10-month-old minority coalition government.

Haidar told a news conference after the talks that the political crisis had not deflected the negotiators, partly because "continuities of policy" tended to outlast government changes. "We were able to continue our work," he said.
"We did reach common ground on a number of issues and aspects," Haidar said. "I will refrain from giving examples."
"The atmosphere of our talks was conducive to serious exchanges. We met in a friendly and cooperative spirit."
The discussions provided a "much more detailed understanding of Pakistan's approach to the talks," he said.

"We believe that we are now much better able to address the issues when we meet again. We hope that our next meeting will take place at an early date," he added. "To be able to discuss things at the level of foreign secretaries is something we have long aspired to and we are glad it happened."

On his arrival at Pakistan's Lahore airport, Ahmad told reporters the talks had been frank and constructive, and said the sides "sought to explore common ground for evolving a mechanism" to address outstanding issues.
"In our interactions, we emphasised the centrality of Jammu and Kashmir dispute in Pakistan-India relations," Ahmad said.
"I stressed that without progress on the core issue of Jammu and Kashmir, meaningful cooperation in the economic and cultural fields between the two countries will be difficult."
Pakistan and India have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir.

Pakistani leaders said before the talks they wanted progress on Kashmir to enable the two sides to move forward on other matters. India made clear it wanted to put Kashmir on hold and focus on trade, economic cooperation and other areas.

Haidar would not specify how the two sides had coped with the decades-old rift over Kashmir during their "wide-ranging" talks. Asked about Pakistan's position that Kashmir must be high on any bilateral agenda, he said simply: "We addressed it."
Haidar said the delegations had spent much time on working out "modalities and structures" for future negotiations.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Gujral has invited his Pakistani opposite number Gohar Ayub to stay on for talks after an April 7-8 Non-Aligned Movement conference in New Delhi.
The two prime ministers may then meet on the sidelines of a summit conference of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation in the Maldives from May 12 to 14.
Haidar said the two sides had discussed the Siachen Glacier, where Indian and Pakistani troops are locked in a high-altitude confrontation, but did not say if anything had been agreed.

He said they had not touched on the idea of extending an existing agreement not to attack each other's nuclear installations or a possible re-opening of the two countries' consulates in Karachi and Bombay.
The question of Pakistan granting most-favoured-nation status in trade to India, which New Delhi has already granted to Islamabad, had been raised, but not discussed in detail.
